title: Where does the fire go?
hookLine: when a fire goes out, did it go north or south? the question doesn't fit

cards: A birthday cake. Someone makes a wish and blows, and the little flames vanish, leaving thin gray ribbons of smoke. A five-year-old at the table asks: where did the fire go?
Everyone laughs. But try answering. It didn't go to the kitchen, or up to the ceiling.

The smoke did, but the smoke isn't the flame. A wanderer named Vacchagotta brings the Buddha a set of hard questions, the same ten from a few days ago, and the Buddha ends up asking him the five-year-old's question.

teach.b: Vacchagotta goes through the list. Is the world eternal? Is it not?
Is the soul the same as the body? Does an awakened one exist after death? To each, the Buddha says: I don't hold that view.
Do you have any view at all, then? The Buddha says he has put away views of that kind. What he has is seeing: how things arise and pass.
Then the hardest one: when a mind is fully freed, where does it reappear?
Reappear doesn't apply, the Buddha says. Doesn't reappear? Doesn't apply.
Both, neither? Doesn't apply. I'm confused, Vacchagotta says.

teach.h: WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?
teach.b: So the Buddha gives him the fire. If a fire were burning in front of you, would you know? Yes.
What is it burning on? Grass and sticks. If it went out, would you know?
Yes. Now, which direction did it go: east, west, north or south? That doesn't apply, Vacchagotta says.
It burned because of its fuel. When the fuel is used up and no more is added, it's simply counted as gone out. That's the answer.

The question was built for things that travel. The word nibbāna, nirvana, draws on this very picture: going out, like a flame. The sutta doesn't say the freed one is annihilated, or that they've gone somewhere else.
It says they're deep and hard to measure, like the ocean. Buddhist schools have discussed this passage for centuries. The fire can't tell you north or south.

how: Buddhist teachers across traditions use the image of a flame going out to explain nirvana, and many temples light candles and lamps on altars as a reminder of the teaching.

o: going out, like a flame when its fuel is spent
the end of a person, wiped out at death
a heavenly place the freed go after death

games.q: the fire and the question: tap the pairs.
p: the wanderer with the hard questions

s: in this sutta the Buddha says a freed one is annihilated at death
he says reappear, not reappear, both and neither all don't apply.
the word nibbāna draws on the image of a flame going out
the sutta's fire simile and the word share that picture.
Vacchagotta admits he's confused before the fire simile
he says he's lost; the fire is the Buddha's answer to that.

games.q: the fire in front of you has gone out. someone asks: did it go east, west, north or south? what do you say?
o: that doesn't apply: it went out when the fuel ran out
games.why: Vacchagotta himself gives this answer, and the Buddha says the same holds for a fully freed one: the question doesn't fit.

practice: If you have a candle nearby and it's safe, light it and watch the flame for a few breaths; if not, picture one, and notice how it depends on the wick and the wax. Then blow it out, or picture it going out, and watch the smoke.
Ask quietly, where did it go, and don't answer: just sit with how the question doesn't fit.

wordCard.voice: Nibbana. When a fire goes out, it didn't go north or south. It went out, because its fuel ran out. The Buddha's picture of nibbāna.

orig.note: Pali nibbāna (Sanskrit nirvāṇa): going out, like a flame whose fuel is spent.

carryVoice: Your line: the question doesn't fit. Some questions are built for things that travel. Until tomorrow.
